Nonparametric Microbial Interdependence Test (NMIT) Distances

Source: R/longitudinal.r
nmit.Rd

Distances between subjects in how their features vary together over time (Zhang et al. 2017), as q2-longitudinal's nmit action computes them: for each subject, the correlation of every pair of features over that subject's samples (its time points); then, for each pair of subjects, a matrix norm of the difference of their correlation matrices. NMIT's test is a PERMANOVA of these distances against a grouping of the subjects: run permanova() on the result.

Usage

nmit(
  counts,
  subjects,
  data = NULL,
  method = "kendall",
  matrix_norm = "frobenius",
  margin = 1L,
  norm = "percent",
  pseudocount = NULL,
  clust = NULL,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

counts

A count table: samples \(\times\) features, or any of the types listed under Input Types. Every sample of a subject enters its correlations, in any order.

subjects

The subject (individual) of each sample: one value per sample, matched to the samples by name when both are named, else in the samples' order; or, with data, the name of one of its columns (q2's individual_id_column). No NAs.

data

Optional sample metadata: a data frame with one row per sample, holding the subjects column. Rows are matched to the samples in counts by row name, and rows for other samples are ignored; without row names, they must be in the samples' order. Default: NULL.

method

The correlation over time: 'kendall' (Kendall's \(\tau_b\), the default, as q2's), 'pearson' or 'spearman'.

matrix_norm

The norm of the difference of two subjects' correlation matrices: 'frobenius' (the default, as q2's) or 'nuclear' (the sum of its singular values).

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

norm

How to normalize counts first: 'percent' (relative abundances, the default, as q2 expects), 'none', 'clr', or any other norm of normalize().

pseudocount

Value added to counts to handle zeros when norm = 'clr' or 'log'. Ignored for other normalization methods. See Pseudocount section.

clust

Whether and how to order the subjects by clustering, as for beta_div(): NULL (the default) or FALSE to keep their order, or one of stats::hclust()'s linkage methods (such as "average"), or "pcoa". The order attribute then gives each subject's position before clustering.

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), is the CPU cores this R process may use, within any limits set on it. Results are the same for any cpus.

Value

A dist object over the subjects (class c("ecodive_dist", "dist")), labelled by subject and in their order (a factor's levels, or sorted), with method "nmit" and title "NMIT Distance". It can be given as dm to permanova(), pcoa() or stats::hclust().

Details

Correlations are computed as pandas' DataFrame.corr() (which q2 calls) computes them. A pair involving a feature that doesn't vary within the subject has no correlation, and counts as 0 (q2's fillna(0)). On the diagonal, pandas puts 1 for Kendall's \(\tau_b\) whatever the feature, but for Pearson and Spearman a constant feature's own correlation is also undefined, so 0: subjects differ there too, and that adds to their distance.

Subjects with fewer than 3 samples have correlations of \(\pm 1\) or 0 only (one sample: none at all), which say little about how their features vary together. q2 computes them all the same; so does nmit(), with a warning naming those subjects. Leave them out first if you can.

Distances: the Frobenius norm of the difference \(\Delta\) is \(\sqrt{2\sum_{a<b} \Delta_{ab}^2 + \sum_a \Delta_{aa}^2}\), computed from the stored lower triangles. The nuclear norm is the sum of the absolute eigenvalues of \(\Delta\) (symmetric, so these are its singular values): an eigendecomposition of a \(D \times D\) matrix for each pair of subjects, \(O(S^2 D^3)\) in all for \(S\) subjects and \(D\) features, which for hundreds of features takes minutes.

Memory: every subject's correlations are kept, \(S D (D + 1) / 2\) numbers (50 subjects and 500 features: 50 MB). nmit() warns above 500 MB; as q2's documentation advises, filter out rare features first.

The test: give permanova() the distances and one group per subject, matched by subject name, for instance from the sample metadata:


  d    <- nmit(counts, 'subject', meta)
  subj <- unique(meta[, c('subject', 'group')])
  rownames(subj) <- subj$subject
  permanova(d, 'group', subj)

Its p-values equal those of other PERMANOVAs of the same distances, such as QIIME 2's beta-group-significance, given the same permutations.

Differences from q2-longitudinal: q2 labels each subject by the ID of its first sample, in the order the subjects first appear; ecodive labels them by subject. Distances are the same to rounding (about \(10^{-15}\)).

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

References

Zhang, Y., Han, S. W., Cox, L. M., & Li, H. (2017). A multivariate distance-based analytic framework for microbial interdependence association test in longitudinal study. Genetic Epidemiology, 41, 769–778. doi:10.1002/gepi.22065

Bokulich, N. A., Dillon, M. R., Zhang, Y., Rideout, J. R., Bolyen, E., Li, H., Albert, P. S., & Caporaso, J. G. (2018). q2-longitudinal: longitudinal and paired-sample analyses of microbiome data. mSystems, 3, e00219-18. doi:10.1128/mSystems.00219-18

See also

Other longitudinal: feature_volatility(), first_differences(), first_distances(), volatility()

Examples

    # Six subjects, each sampled 5 times; two diets.
    meta <- data.frame(
      subject = rep(sprintf('m%d', 1:6), each = 5),
      diet    = rep(c('x', 'y'), each = 15) )
    counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 6, 30), 30, dimnames = list(NULL, letters[1:6]))

    d <- nmit(counts, 'subject', meta)
    d
#> # A dist: 6 subjects (lower triangle)
#> # NMIT Distance
#>      m1   m2   m3   m4   m5
#> m2 3.62
#> m3 3.39 2.04
#> m4 2.94 3.05 3.67
#> m5 3.97 3.01 3.26 2.73
#> m6 3.76 3.21 3.16 3.41 3.05
#> # Attributes: method

    # NMIT's test: a PERMANOVA of the subjects.
    subj <- unique(meta)
    rownames(subj) <- subj$subject
    permanova(d, 'diet', subj, permutations = 99)
#> Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) of NMIT Distance
#> 
#> F = 1.546, p = 0.22, z = 1.207
#> Permutations: 99 (free)
#> 
#> Model R2 = 0.2788. Model tested as a whole:
#> 
#>          Df SumOfSqs     R2     F Pr(>F)
#> Model     1     7.36 0.2788 1.546   0.22
#> Residual  4    19.04 0.7212             
#> Total     5    26.40 1.0000
